classification: Actual final v6 learned EV content contradicts some original TRAIN target branches; separates rule-content defects from execution lapses. Pinned metadata read for diagnosis only, never actor/teacher input or rescoring.

ARIZONA.when: When ARIZONA is allowable and an asset is tested against an Arizona substantive exemption.
ARIZONA.procedure: Match the asset before valuing it: use § 33-1101(A) for an occupied homestead, § 33-1123 for household furniture, goods, electronics, or appliances, § 33-1125(1) for actual wearing apparel, (4) only for engagement or wedding rings, (6) for one watch, (8) for one motor vehicle, (9) for a professionally prescribed prosthesis or physician-authorized mobility or respiratory aid, (10) for firearms, and (11) for domestic animals or household pets. For the whole named asset use the smaller of its value and $400,000 under § 33-1101(A), $15,000 under § 33-1123 or (8), $500 under (1), $2,000 under (4) or (10), or $250 under (6). The supplied provisions state no dollar ceiling for qualifying property under (9) or (11).
ARIZONA.avoid_when: Do not cite § 33-1101(B) or § 33-1121 as an asset exemption. Do not classify jewelry, a prescribed medical device, or another item as household goods merely because it is kept at home. A pendant, necklace, bracelet, cocktail ring, or anniversary ring is not wearing apparel and does not qualify as an engagement or wedding ring without those facts.

FEDERAL.when: When FEDERAL is allowable and an estate asset is being valued.
FEDERAL.procedure: For each asset, first select every matching specific paragraph: (d)(1) for an occupied residence, (d)(2) for a motor vehicle, (d)(3) only for its listed household-use categories, (d)(4) for jewelry, (d)(6) only when the facts establish a trade implement, professional book, or tool, and (d)(9) for a professionally prescribed health aid. Separately add (d)(5) to every asset, even one already receiving a specific exemption. For each citation use the smaller of the whole named asset's value and its ceiling: $27,900 for (d)(1), $4,450 for (d)(2), $700 for the named particular item under (d)(3), $1,875 for (d)(4), and $2,800 for (d)(6); (d)(9) has no stated ceiling. For (d)(5), use $15,425 for one debtor or $30,850 for two equal joint debtors when no used homestead amount is supplied. Because this task evaluates asset-exemption pairs independently, do not reduce that amount merely because the same case also contains a residence claim.
FEDERAL.avoid_when: Do not put firearms or jewelry under (d)(3), and do not infer (d)(6) without stated trade use. Treat a pair or set presented as one named asset as one particular item for the $700 (d)(3) output. Never copy a ceiling above the asset's value, leave a half-interest as the result, or use the one-debtor (d)(5) ceiling for two equal joint debtors. Do not output §§ 522(b), 522(d), or 522(m) as asset exemptions.

ILLINOIS.when: When ILLINOIS is allowable and the debtor owns personal-use personal property.
ILLINOIS.procedure: Use two independent passes. First add 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) for every personal-use personal-property asset, including apparel, a vehicle, or a prescribed health aid; the words “any other property” do not make (b) mutually exclusive with a specific alternative. Its whole-asset amount is the smaller of the asset value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for two equal joint debtors. Second add each factually matching specific provision: (a) for necessary wearing apparel, (c) for a motor vehicle with a $2,400 asset-level ceiling, (d) only for facts stating trade use with a $1,500 ceiling, and (e) for a professionally prescribed health aid. Provisions (a) and (e) retain the asset value because they state no dollar ceiling.
ILLINOIS.avoid_when: Do not apply these alternatives to property stated to be business-use. Do not omit (b) when a specific provision applies. Do not infer (d) from the object's form, name, tool loops, or possible usefulness; the facts must establish use in the debtor's trade. Do not double the (c) ceiling or classify jewelry as necessary wearing apparel.

ALL.when: For every EV asset after the allowable legal namespaces have been supplied.
ALL.procedure: Test every substantive exemption independently. Retain every qualifying specific, wildcard, and general-property alternative together, emitting each citation once. For each alternative, report the protected amount for the whole named asset, limited by that asset's value and that provision's applicable ceiling.
ALL.avoid_when: Do not cite enabling, opt-out, marital-coordination, or aggregate-limit provisions as asset exemptions. Do not omit a general alternative because a specific one applies. Do not leave a half-interest as the final amount or automatically double every ceiling merely because two debtors exist; apply the joint treatment stated for the particular provision.

OREGON.when: When OREGON is allowable and an asset is being valued.
OREGON.procedure: For every personal-property asset, add § 18.345(1)(p) with the smaller of its whole value and $400, then independently add each matching specific alternative: (1)(a) for books, pictures, or musical instruments capped at $600; (1)(b) for wearing apparel or jewelry capped at $1,800; (1)(d) for a vehicle capped at $3,000; (1)(e) for family-use domestic animals or poultry capped at $1,000; (1)(f) for household goods, furniture, radios, a television, or utensils capped at $3,000; (1)(h) for professionally prescribed health aids with no stated ceiling; and § 18.362 for one qualifying firearm capped at $1,000. For an occupied homestead use § 18.395(1), capped at $40,000 for one debtor or $50,000 for joint household debtors, and do not add (1)(p).
OREGON.avoid_when: Use the smaller of the asset value and each ceiling; never output the ceiling when the asset is worth less. Do not classify apparel under household goods, or a household appliance under apparel. Do not omit a matching specific category merely because (1)(p) applies, automatically double the listed asset-level ceilings, or output § 18.345(3) as an asset exemption.

PENNSYLVANIA.when: When PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
PENNSYLVANIA.procedure: Add 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 independently to every asset alongside all qualifying federal or specific Pennsylvania alternatives. Use the smaller of the whole asset value and $300 for one debtor or $600 for two equal joint debtors; determine which ceiling applies from the stated debtor count. Add § 8124(a)(1) only for actual wearing apparel, (a)(2) only for a Bible or school book, (a)(3) only for the specified family or seamstress sewing machine, and (a)(4) only for an actual military uniform or accoutrement.
PENNSYLVANIA.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because another exemption applies, use $600 for a single debtor, or copy a ceiling above the asset value. A firearm, jewelry item, vehicle, household textile, or other carried or household object does not become wearing apparel or military accoutrement without the required facts.

WISCONSIN.when: When WISCONSIN is allowable and an asset is being valued.
WISCONSIN.procedure: For listed nonvehicle consumer goods, including firearms, use § 815.18(3)(d), capped for the whole asset at $12,000 for one debtor or $24,000 for two equal joint debtors. For a motor vehicle, output only § 815.18(3)(g), not a separate (d) claim. Because this independent-pair task supplies no used consumer-goods amount, treat the (d) amount as unused: the single (g) claim has a $16,000 ceiling for one debtor or $32,000 for two equal joint debtors. Use § 815.20(1) only for an occupied homestead, capped at $75,000 for one debtor or $150,000 for two joint spouses. For each citation output the smaller of the whole asset value and its ceiling.
WISCONSIN.avoid_when: Do not put a motor vehicle under (3)(d) or split its combined vehicle protection into separate (3)(g) and (3)(d) claims. A firearm is consumer goods under (3)(d), not a depository account under (3)(k) or business property under (3)(b)(1) without the required facts. Do not emit § 815.18(8), leave a half-interest as the result, or stop at one spouse's ceiling for jointly owned property where both spouses' exemptions apply.
